method: Literal question and answer-rationale review across the complete 240-entry records. Targeted fresh primary-source reading concentrated on restored answers and questionable older inferences. Existing unknown entries remain unresolved; this review does not claim exhaustive new research on every unknown. Source absence was not encoded as zero. Scores were not consulted.
sourceReadChecks: Liberal International Andorra 2017 and marriage reform 2002, indexed full text; 2012 LGBTI principles considered with the stated equality inference.
TRG King’s Speech 6 November 2023 and Hong Kong BNO campaign 28 May 2020, full indexed text.
Hobhouse Social Evolution and Political Theory: social transmission, inherited capacities, and the distinction between social and racial progress; modest Culture/Nature inferences retained.
US AI Action Plan July 2025: workforce displacement provisions retained; environmental permitting did not establish the two habitat/uncertainty tradeoffs.
Kristol 1983 interview and 2003 Neoconservative Persuasion: mixed redistribution/planning retained; alternative delivery does not establish private contractor preference.
National Conservatism 2022 principles, all ten sections: religious public morality and federal exceptions retained; deterrence distinguished from supremacy and an exclusive armed-attack rule.
Duniam 21 July 2026 immigration speech: housing ceiling, temporary status and common civic obligations retained as opposition programme, not incumbent acts.

Thatcher 1979 manifesto, Right Approach, UN environmental speech and 1988 Christianity speech: immigration temporary-settlement rule and national core curriculum retained; tax-band differentiation directly contradicts inferred flat marginal rates.

NOW Issues Manual: CAFTA pp89–92, progressive taxation p194, welfare pp44–46, national rights floor p196, local CEDAW and health campaigns, religion/church-state sections; adopted 2021 foreign-policy and draft abolition resolutions; 2007 immigration principles; SEP liberal feminism autonomy, sex education and gradualism passages.
limitations: Review completion is not assessment completion. No revision was archived, no catalogue was regenerated and no percentages were restored.

profiles.scope: US egalitarian liberal feminism represented by NOW and scholarship. Unsupported extensions beyond the cited programme remain unknown. Government acts are context, not a substitute for evidence of this tradition.

changes.question: My country should maintain forces capable of prolonged combat beyond its borders.

before.rationale: Documented mixed commitment: NOW opposed prolonged unilateral occupation of Iraq and US troop expansion, while calling for larger international peacekeeping forces in Afghanistan and a multinational force in Iraq (Issues Manual pp89–90,190–191). Overseas capacity is supported for peacekeeping but rejected for occupation; neither blanket proposition fits.

after.rationale: Unresolved after independent source review: NOW supports some international peacekeeping missions while opposing occupations. Those positions do not settle maintaining national forces capable of prolonged combat overseas; mission purpose and combat capacity are different questions.

changes.question: International human-rights institutions should be able to require changes to my country’s laws.

before.rationale: NOW expressly advocates ratifying CEDAW without limiting reservations and implementing its requirements in domestic law (Issues Manual pp67–68; adopted 2021 foreign-policy resolution). This is support for accepting substantive international human-rights obligations, not a claim every international body has unilateral domestic authority.

after.rationale: Unresolved after independent source review: Ratifying and implementing CEDAW accepts treaty obligations. That does not itself establish granting international institutions authority to require domestic legal changes; treaty commitment and institutional compulsory jurisdiction are distinct.

changes.question: My country should remove most barriers to international trade, even when some domestic businesses lose sales.

before.rationale: The 2004 resolution supports fair trade but opposes CAFTA because its liberalisation model weakens wages, bargaining power and access to services (Issues Manual pp90–91). Infer qualified disagreement with removing most barriers simply despite domestic losses, rather than opposition to all international exchange.

after.rationale: Unresolved after independent source review: The CAFTA resolution objects to labour conditions, relocation and unequal gains. It does not settle removing most import barriers despite domestic firms losing sales.

changes.question: Businesses in my country should be free to buy goods and materials from whichever country offers the best terms.

before.rationale: NOW explicitly places fair trade, labour rights and sustainable development above unrestricted relocation and sourcing on purely commercial terms in its 2004 CAFTA resolution (Issues Manual pp90–91). Infer a qualified rejection of choosing suppliers solely on best terms. No general import embargo is inferred.

after.rationale: Unresolved after independent source review: Opposing exploitative relocation does not settle freedom to purchase foreign goods on the best terms; production location and sourcing restrictions are distinct.

changes.question: Trade agreements signed by my country should remove tariffs, even when this increases dependence on foreign suppliers.

before.rationale: The explicit rejection of CAFTA and criticism of the NAFTA model on wages and service access supports qualified disagreement with treating tariff removal as a sufficient objective despite greater dependence. This does not prescribe exact tariff levels.

after.rationale: Unresolved after independent source review: The CAFTA criticism does not establish a position on removing tariffs despite dependence on foreign suppliers. Labour protections and supplier dependence are different trade-offs.

changes.question: Higher earners in my country should pay a substantially larger share of their income in tax than lower earners.

before.rationale: NOW opposes the 2001 tax-cut distribution favouring the richest households over low-paid women (Issues Manual pp193–194), together with an egalitarian commitment to adequate social support. Infer progressive income-tax burdens, without inventing specific brackets.

after.rationale: NOW’s 2001 tax resolution calls for progressive payroll taxation with higher rates for higher incomes and removing the taxable-income cap (Issues Manual p194). This supports a qualified larger proportional burden without inventing brackets.

changes.question: Additional income earned by high earners should not face higher tax rates than additional income earned by other workers.

before.rationale: Opposition to disproportionate tax relief for top earners and support for adequately funded welfare (Issues Manual pp193–194,44–46) supports qualified rejection of identical marginal burdens regardless of high earnings. This is a normative inference, not a published tax-rate schedule.

after.rationale: NOW’s 2001 tax resolution explicitly proposes progressive payroll rates increasing with income and removing the cap (Issues Manual p194). This supports rejection of identical marginal tax rates, more directly than general opposition to tax cuts.

changes.question: My country should recognise decisions made by religious courts as legally binding in some areas of family law.

before.rationale: The equal-rights and personal-autonomy commitments reject family-law decisions binding a person through a religious authority rather than civil law. Qualified disagreement allows voluntary private religious advice without making it legally binding.

after.rationale: Unresolved after independent source review: Equal civil rights and church-state separation do not by themselves settle legally binding religious arbitration freely chosen by all adults, with possible civil oversight.

changes.question: Traditional expectations about modest dress should continue to guide how people dress in public.

before.rationale: The egalitarian liberal-feminist personal-autonomy account lets women choose their own conception of the good and rejects enforced gender conventions. Infer qualified disagreement with traditional modesty expectations as the governing public standard, without prescribing that individuals abandon voluntary modest dress.

after.rationale: Unresolved after independent source review: Autonomy opposes coercive dress rules, but this statement concerns traditional expectations guiding public dress. The sources do not settle voluntary modesty norms as phrased.

changes.question: Changes to long-standing social institutions should be gradual, even when faster change is popular.

before.rationale: NOW seeks legal and institutional equality immediately and rejects barriers sustained by custom; the liberal-feminist account justifies reform by equal autonomy rather than the age of an institution. Infer qualified disagreement with a general requirement of gradual change when reform is justified, not unconditional endorsement of every popular rapid change.

after.rationale: Unresolved after independent source review: Calls for prompt equality reforms do not establish a general position on the pace of every long-standing social institution. Liberal feminist scholarship also describes gradual experimentation; neither establishes the question’s general priority.

changes.question: States and regions should have a protected right to govern their own affairs, even when the national government disagrees with their policies.

before.rationale: Documented mix: NOW endorses local and state CEDAW implementation and state single-payer initiatives, while opposing state derogation from national employment and equality rights (Issues Manual pp63–68,108–109,194–196). Regional initiative is protected subject to national rights, rather than always subordinate or always immune.

after.rationale: Unresolved after independent source review: Local CEDAW campaigns and state health initiatives show action at several levels, not a protected regional power to decide policy against national disagreement.

changes.question: The national government should decide which medical treatments public healthcare covers, even if regional governments would cover different treatments.

before.rationale: Documented institutional mix: NOW advocates national comprehensive single-payer coverage and explicitly endorses state single-payer laws as a route to it (Issues Manual pp36–37,108–109). National coverage protections coexist with legitimate state initiatives, so neither exclusive national control nor unrestricted regional divergence is prescribed.

after.rationale: Unresolved after independent source review: National and state single-payer campaigns do not settle whether national government should determine covered treatments when regional governments disagree.

sourceIssues: Some Liberal International/TRG pages failed direct opening; indexed full-page text was read instead where available. No numeric answer was accepted on an inaccessible URL alone.
General doctrine supports normative inference, but not unspecified thresholds, comparative causal claims, or replacing the question with a related policy.
